name: BABOK® Guide v3 — a twelve-week programme
strap: The whole guide, in the order a study group works it. Each week explains the ground, names what the exam tests, and drills it.
intro: Twelve weeks covers the BABOK Guide v3 end to end: the key concepts that hold it together, the six knowledge areas in the order that makes them easiest to learn, and the perspectives that sit behind them. Each week is written to be read before a session and used during one.

Every week names the tasks in scope, the concepts worth being precise about, the techniques that belong to that session, and the traps the exam sets. Then it drills you on exactly that ground, and hands you blank templates for the techniques so you can use them on real work rather than only recognise them in a question.
note: Written from the BABOK Guide v3 structure. All explanation, questions and templates here are original: no BABOK text is reproduced, and nothing is drawn from any particular study group's materials.

weeks.title: Introduction and the core concept model
weeks.strap: Six concepts that constrain each other. Get these right and the rest of the guide reads as one argument.
overview: The guide opens by defining what business analysis is and then gives you the model everything else hangs from: the Business Analysis Core Concept Model. Six concepts — change, need, solution, stakeholder, value and context — none of which can be settled on its own.

That interdependence is the whole point and it is the thing most often skipped. A candidate who treats the six as a list to memorise will miss the questions built on them, because those questions turn on what happens to the other five when one of them moves. Spend this week getting comfortable holding all six at once.

concepts.meaning: A controlled transformation of an enterprise in response to a need. Control and intent are what separate a change from a variation in conditions — a storm-driven spike in volume is not a change, a deliberate reorganisation is.
A problem or opportunity to be addressed. Needs motivate change; they are not the same as the wants stakeholders express, and stating one as a solution is the most common error in the guide.
A specific way of satisfying one or more needs in a context. Note the last three words: the same solution can be right in one context and wrong in another.
A group or individual with a relationship to the change, the need or the solution. Considerably wider than users — a regulator that constrains the solution is a stakeholder.
The worth of something to a stakeholder in a context. It can be a loss avoided or an obligation met, and it can be negative. Not confined to money.
The circumstances that influence, are influenced by, and provide understanding of the change. Not everything true about the enterprise — the test is whether a fact would change a decision.

traps: Treating one concept as decidable alone. If the context turns out to be four distribution centres rather than one, the stakeholders and the solution both change with it.
Reading value as revenue. A compliance change with no return still delivers value: the licence retained, the loss avoided.
Reading stakeholder as user. Anyone with a relationship to the change qualifies, including parties who only constrain or test it.
Widening context until it means nothing. A description that includes everything discriminates nothing.
prepare: Read chapters 1 and 2 of the guide.
Take a change you are working on now and write one sentence for each of the six concepts. Notice which one you find hardest — for most people it is value or context.
Bring an example where a change in context forced the solution to change.
discuss: Which of the six is hardest to pin down on your own work, and why?
Give an example of value that was not money. How did you get it accepted?
Where have you seen a need stated as a solution, and what did it cost?

weeks.title: Key concepts and requirements classification
weeks.strap: Requirement against design, and the four classes. Two distinctions that the exam returns to again and again.
overview: The second half of chapter 2 gives you two distinctions worth being exact about. The first is requirement against design. A requirement is a usable representation of a need; a design is a usable representation of a solution. What separates them is intent — not level of detail, not which phase produced them, not the notation.

The second is the classification schema: business, stakeholder, solution — functional and non-functional — and transition. Getting this right matters because the class determines who owns a requirement, how it is validated, and in the case of transition requirements, when it stops applying.

concepts.meaning: A usable representation of a need. It says what is needed, not how it will be met.
A usable representation of a solution. Both are elaborated in parallel throughout, and both are legitimate business analysis outputs.
A goal or objective of the enterprise. Reducing processing cost by 20% within two years.
The need of a particular group. Assessors need to see restriction data while assessing.
What the solution must do (functional) or how well it must do it (non-functional). A quality with no measure attached is an aspiration, not a requirement.
Needed only to move from current to future state. It lapses once the change is complete, which is why they should be closed rather than carried forward for years.

traps: Judging requirement against design by how detailed it is. A one-line statement can be a design; a page of prose can be a requirement.
Assuming the distinction maps onto project phases. A mock-up produced during analysis is still a design.
Classifying by who raised it. A goal of the enterprise is a business requirement whoever mentions it.
Leaving transition requirements open after go-live, so the repository stops describing anything true.
prepare: Read the rest of chapter 2, particularly the requirements classification schema.
Take ten statements from a real requirements document and classify each. Note the ones you argue with yourself about.
Find a statement in your own work that is really a design labelled as a requirement.
discuss: Where does your organisation draw the line between requirement and design, and does it hold?
What happens to transition requirements in your shop after cutover?
Has a vocabulary dispute ever been mistaken for a requirements dispute on your work?

weeks.title: Strategy Analysis, part 1
weeks.strap: Understand where the enterprise is before describing where it should go. Diagnosis before design.
overview: Strategy analysis is where a change is justified rather than specified. The first half is current state and future state: understanding the enterprise as it is, why it underperforms, and then describing the state that would satisfy the need.

The discipline this week is not jumping. Analysing the current state is diagnosis, and an item that moves from a recurring failure straight to a fix is testing whether you stopped to find the cause. Equally, the future state is a description of a state, not a plan for getting there — that comes next week.

tasks.name: Analyze Current State
tasks.what: Understand the enterprise as it is: its needs, capabilities, structure, culture, and the external environment it operates in.
tasks.watch: This task diagnoses. It does not design, and it does not choose. If the answer proposes a solution, check whether the cause has been established.

tasks.name: Define Future State
tasks.what: Describe the state that would meet the need, with objectives set well enough to tell whether you got there.
tasks.watch: A future state is a description, not a delivery plan. Objectives need to be measurable or the change cannot be evaluated later.

concepts.meaning: The problem or opportunity of consequence to the enterprise. Everything in strategy analysis traces back to it.
What the enterprise is able to do, independently of who does it or how. Capabilities cut across departments, which is why departmental fixes leave enterprise symptoms untouched.
The value a future state could deliver. Assessed before commitment, and revisited when the context moves.
The boundary of what a solution will address. Defined here well enough to estimate, refined later.

traps: Designing the future state while describing the current one.
Confusing internal weakness with external threat. Lacking a capability is a weakness; a competitor exploiting that lack is the threat.
Comparing yourself only with yourself. A claim about being uncompetitive needs an outside reference point.
Framing an enterprise-wide symptom as a departmental process problem, then fixing three departments and wondering why nothing moved.
prepare: Read 6.1 and 6.2.
Sketch a capability view of your own organisation — six to ten capabilities, graded for performance and importance. Notice how different it looks from the org chart.
Bring a current-state finding you had to defend to someone who wanted to skip to the solution.
discuss: How does your organisation decide a need is worth acting on?
Where have you seen a solution chosen before the need was agreed, and how did it end?
Capability or process — which framing gets more traction with your executives, and why?

weeks.title: Strategy Analysis, part 2
weeks.strap: Risk and the change strategy. This is the week the numbers show up.
overview: Having described where the enterprise is and where it should be, the second half of strategy analysis assesses what could go wrong on the way and settles how the change will be made. This is where financial analysis, decision analysis and risk work sit, and where most candidates find the arithmetic they have been avoiding.

The exam leans hard on two things here. First, that mitigation changes a risk rather than closing it — residual risk has to be accepted explicitly. Second, that a positive return is not the same as the best option: expect to be shown something profitable that is beaten by an alternative, or that fails against the cost of capital.

tasks.name: Assess Risks
tasks.what: Identify uncertain events that could affect value, assess likelihood and impact, and settle a response for each.
tasks.watch: A risk is an uncertain future event; an issue is already happening. Responses are avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept or increase — not simply escalate.

tasks.name: Define Change Strategy
tasks.what: Choose the approach to the change: the options, the recommended one, the gaps to be closed and the transition states.
tasks.watch: The strategy explains how the enterprise will get from here to there, including what happens in between. Options that were rejected belong in it.

concepts.meaning: What remains after a response is applied. Mitigation moves a risk on the grid; it does not remove it from the grid, and accepting what remains must be a decision on the record.
Each outcome weighted by its likelihood. The figure that belongs in a business case, while the severe case belongs in the risk register.
Discounted benefits less discounted costs. Positive means the option beat the cost of capital — a raw surplus can still be a negative NPV.
An intermediate state the enterprise passes through. Real changes rarely go from current to future in one move.

traps: Comparing undiscounted totals when the options differ mainly in timing.
Reading a ratio as a size. A 300% return on $10,000 is a smaller prize than 50% on $500,000.
Treating a short payback as decisive when the constraint is value rather than cash exposure.
Letting money already spent influence a forward-looking choice.
Closing a risk because a monitoring alert was added. Detection is not prevention.
prepare: Read 6.3 and 6.4.
Work one NPV by hand: discount each year separately, then add. If you can do that, most of the financial questions become arithmetic rather than judgement.
Bring a business case you have written or reviewed, and be ready to say what it left out.
discuss: How does your organisation set its hurdle rate, and does anyone check options against it?
Where have you seen sunk cost drive a decision?
Which risks get recorded in your shop, and which get carried as optimism?

weeks.title: Solution Evaluation
weeks.strap: Did it work, and if not, is the fault inside the solution or in the enterprise around it?
overview: Solution evaluation asks whether the thing that was built is delivering the value that justified it. It runs on solutions already in use, and on ones still in construction, and it is the knowledge area candidates most often underestimate because it looks like reporting. It is not.

The distinction that carries this chapter is where a limitation sits. A solution can be working exactly as designed and still deliver nothing, because the enterprise around it has not changed. Telling those two apart decides which task you are in and what you would recommend, and the exam tests it repeatedly.

tasks.name: Measure Solution Performance
tasks.what: Decide what will be measured and how, so performance can be judged rather than asserted.
tasks.watch: Without a baseline there is no improvement to claim. Measures also need targets and thresholds, or they produce reporting rather than management.

tasks.name: Analyze Performance Measures
tasks.what: Interpret the measures against the expected value and say what they mean.
tasks.watch: Gross benefit is not realised benefit. Run cost, and any cost that has not yet stopped, come off before anything is claimed.

tasks.name: Assess Solution Limitations
tasks.what: Find what is constraining performance inside the solution itself.
tasks.watch: Defects, missing function, unusable design — things you would fix by changing the solution.

tasks.name: Assess Enterprise Limitations
tasks.what: Find what is constraining performance outside the solution: structure, culture, policy, capability.
tasks.watch: A perfectly built solution nobody is trained, incentivised or permitted to use is limited by the enterprise, not by itself.

tasks.name: Recommend Actions to Increase Solution Value
tasks.what: Say what should be done: adjust, replace, retire, or change the enterprise around it.
tasks.watch: Doing nothing is a legitimate recommendation and should appear when it is the right one.

concepts.meaning: The measured value before the change. Without it, improvement is an assertion. Establishing one is part of 8.1, not an afterthought.
A lagging indicator confirms an outcome after it is too late to change it. A dashboard of only lagging measures cannot support intervention.
Hours released that never leave the budget. Real, but not a saving until establishment falls, bought-in spend drops, or the capacity absorbs work you would otherwise have paid for.
A constraint within the solution. Contrast with an enterprise limitation, which sits in the organisation around it.

traps: Reading gross benefit as net. Run cost and double-running cost come off first.
Optimising one dimension because the measures that would show the cost are absent — a balanced scorecard exists to catch exactly that.
Calling an enterprise limitation a solution defect, and rebuilding something that works.
Claiming hours saved as money when headcount and budget are unchanged.
prepare: Read chapter 8.
Take a solution you have delivered and ask what its baseline was. If you cannot answer, that is the lesson.
Bring an example where the solution worked and the benefit did not arrive.
discuss: Who owns benefit realisation in your organisation, and does it survive go-live?
Have you seen a non-cashable benefit claimed as a saving? What happened at audit?
Where did an enterprise limitation get mistaken for a system problem?

weeks.title: Elicitation and Collaboration
weeks.strap: Choosing the instrument is most of the skill. Depth or breadth, stated or observed, discussion or decision.
overview: Elicitation is drawing out information; collaboration is keeping the people involved engaged while you do it. The chapter covers preparing, conducting, confirming what you got, communicating it, and managing the relationships that make any of it possible.

Most questions here turn on picking the right instrument for the situation. Interviews go deep with a few people and can ask the follow-up question; surveys go wide and cannot. Observation catches what people cannot articulate or do not realise they do. Workshops produce an agreed output; focus groups produce opinion. Read the scenario for what is actually needed and the choice usually settles itself.

tasks.name: Prepare for Elicitation
tasks.what: Scope the activity, pick the technique, arrange the logistics and the participants.
tasks.watch: Document analysis belongs here. Time with a scarce expert is wasted on questions the documents already answer.

tasks.name: Conduct Elicitation
tasks.what: Draw the information out.
tasks.watch: The technique has to match the information sought — tacit expertise is not reachable by questionnaire.

tasks.name: Confirm Elicitation Results
tasks.what: Check what you captured against other sources and with the people who gave it.
tasks.watch: Two records that appear to conflict are often one word carrying two meanings.

tasks.name: Communicate Business Analysis Information
tasks.what: Get the information to stakeholders in a form they can act on.
tasks.watch: The form follows the audience and the decision, not the analyst's preference.

tasks.name: Manage Stakeholder Collaboration
tasks.what: Keep stakeholders engaged through the work.
tasks.watch: Disengagement usually follows a failure of follow-through, not of facilitation. Concerns raised with no owner teach people not to raise them.

concepts.meaning: Expertise the holder has never articulated. Reachable by interview and observation, not by a fixed instrument.
The people who chose to respond. A banner survey on a portal reaches those the portal worked for, which is why a low response rate can be flattering rather than merely thin.
A facilitated session with a stated output, the people who can agree it, and a scribe. Missing any of those and it is a meeting.

traps: Reaching for breadth when the need is depth, or the reverse.
Believing the documented procedure over the work as performed.
Treating a vocabulary dispute as a requirements conflict.
Blaming facilitation when the real failure is that nothing happened after the session.
prepare: Read chapter 4.
Write the first five questions you would put to a subject-matter expert you had ninety minutes with, and mark which ones a document could answer.
Bring a session that went badly and be ready to say which instrument would have suited it better.
discuss: What is the most useful elicitation you have ever done, and why did it work?
How do you handle a stakeholder who agrees in the room and objects afterwards?
Where does information go to die in your organisation?

weeks.title: Requirements Analysis and Design Definition, part 1
weeks.strap: The largest knowledge area on the exam. Specify, verify, validate — and know which is which.
overview: RADD is thirty per cent of the blueprint, more than any other area, and it splits neatly into two halves. The first is specifying and modelling requirements, then checking them twice: verification and validation.

Those two checks are the most confused pair in the guide. Verification asks whether the requirement is well written — unambiguous, testable, consistent. Validation asks whether it delivers value and aligns to the business need. Both can be done with a review, so the question is never which technique was used; it is what the reviewers were asked to judge, and whether the right people were in the room.

tasks.name: Specify and Model Requirements
tasks.what: Express requirements and designs in a form fit for the audience: text, matrices, diagrams, models.
tasks.watch: The notation follows the subject. Hand-offs between people point to a process model; statuses point to a state model; ordered messages between components point to a sequence diagram.

tasks.name: Verify Requirements
tasks.what: Check the requirement is well specified and of sufficient quality to work from.
tasks.watch: A well-written requirement can still be the wrong one. Verification cannot detect that.

tasks.name: Validate Requirements
tasks.what: Check the requirement delivers value and supports the business objectives.
tasks.watch: Needs the business in the room. Testers verifying among themselves will pass obsolete requirements.

concepts.meaning: Are we building it right — is this requirement well formed?
Are we building the right thing — does this requirement still deliver value?
What a use case carries beyond the happy path. Their absence is why so much gets discovered during testing.
Different notations answer different questions. A data flow diagram follows information; a process model follows work; they are not interchangeable.

traps: Treating verification as sufficient. A third of a requirements set can be obsolete and still pass a quality review.
Specifying only the successful path and calling the requirement complete.
Choosing a notation because the team prefers it rather than because it expresses the subject.
Burying a volatile policy inside the workflow that applies it.
prepare: Read 7.1 to 7.3.
Take one requirement and write its alternate and exception flows. Most people find more than they expected.
Bring a model you have drawn and be ready to say why that notation and not another.
discuss: Who validates requirements in your organisation, and are they the right people?
Which notation do you reach for by habit rather than by fit?
Where have business rules ended up hard-coded, and what did the next policy change cost?

weeks.title: Requirements Analysis and Design Definition, part 2
weeks.strap: Architecture, options and the recommendation. Where analysis turns into a decision.
overview: The second half of RADD structures the requirements as a whole, defines the design options that could meet them, and recommends one on the basis of value. It is where the analysis work of the previous weeks is brought to a point.

The recurring examinable distinction is between analysing potential value and planning delivery. Producing a work breakdown, a schedule or a resourcing profile for the options is project management. The analyst owes a value-based recommendation, and being asked for a delivery plan instead is one of the most frequently set traps in the guide.

tasks.name: Define Requirements Architecture
tasks.what: Structure the requirements so they fit together, cover the need and can be traced.
tasks.watch: Gaps and inconsistencies between requirements are found here, not in a single requirement's wording.

tasks.name: Define Design Options
tasks.what: Identify ways of meeting the need, including improving the current state, and describe each well enough to compare.
tasks.watch: Doing nothing, and improving what exists, are options. A single costed option is not a set.

tasks.name: Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution
tasks.what: Assess the value each option could deliver and recommend one.
tasks.watch: This is the value question, not the delivery question. Watch for a plausible option that is beaten, or that fails against the cost of capital.

concepts.meaning: The requirements as a structured whole, with the relationships between them, rather than a list.
A way of meeting the need. Must include enough detail to be compared, and the set must include the alternatives that were genuinely considered.
Acquisition plus operating, support and disposal, over the whole life. The purchase price is rarely the decision.
What is given up by choosing one option. A recommendation without one has usually not been analysed.

traps: Producing a delivery schedule when a value recommendation was owed.
Specifying what crosses a boundary before agreeing where the boundary is.
Assessing the product and forgetting the supplier behind it.
Leaving quality attributes to be settled by the technical team during design, after the architecture is chosen.
prepare: Read 7.4 to 7.6.
Take a recent solution decision and write the option set as it should have been — including doing nothing.
Bring a set of non-functional requirements and check whether every one carries a number.
discuss: How are design options generated in your organisation, and by whom?
When did you last see doing nothing seriously assessed?
Who decides the quality attributes where you work?

weeks.title: Requirements Life Cycle Management
weeks.strap: Keeping requirements usable from the moment they appear to long after they are delivered.
overview: This chapter is about custody. Requirements are traced to what justifies them and what implements them, kept current as things change, ordered so the most valuable work comes first, assessed when someone proposes a change, and formally approved.

The examinable heart of it is prioritisation. Value is one basis among several, and it is not always the governing one. A regulatory deadline, a dependency, a risk or an implementation constraint can each outrank it, and an item that hands you a statutory date and then asks you to rank on business value is testing exactly that.

tasks.name: Trace Requirements
tasks.what: Maintain the relationships between requirements, designs, solution components and the objectives they serve.
tasks.watch: Tracing is what lets you answer 'why does this exist' and 'what breaks if it changes'.

tasks.name: Maintain Requirements
tasks.what: Keep requirements accurate and reusable over time, including after delivery.
tasks.watch: A backlog of items that describe changes is not a statement of the current state. Both are needed.

tasks.name: Prioritize Requirements
tasks.what: Order requirements against an agreed basis.
tasks.watch: The basis matters more than the ranking. Value, risk, dependency, regulatory deadline, cost and difficulty are all legitimate bases.

tasks.name: Assess Requirements Changes
tasks.what: Evaluate a proposed change for its effect on value, on other requirements, and on the work.
tasks.watch: The assessment is of impact, not of whether the requester is entitled to ask.

tasks.name: Approve Requirements
tasks.what: Obtain agreement from the people with authority to give it.
tasks.watch: Approval needs the right authority, which means knowing where decision rights actually sit.

concepts.meaning: The relationships that let a requirement be followed up to its justification and down to its implementation.
What the ordering is against. Naming it is what makes a ranking defensible to whoever loses out.
The ongoing custody of the list. Distinct from prioritisation, which is the act of ordering it.
An approved set, held so that later change can be assessed against something fixed.

traps: Ranking on value when a dependency or a statutory date governs.
Re-prioritising a list a third of which is obsolete, and producing a well-ordered list of the wrong work.
Confusing an issue with a risk. An issue is already happening.
Approving with whoever is available rather than whoever holds the mandate.
prepare: Read chapter 5.
Look at your current backlog and estimate what share of it no longer represents a live need.
Bring a prioritisation decision that was overturned, and be ready to say on what basis it had been made.
discuss: What is your organisation's real basis for prioritisation, as opposed to its stated one?
How would you answer an auditor asking what the current rule is and when it last changed?
Who can approve a requirement where you work, and does everyone agree on that?

weeks.title: Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, part 1
weeks.strap: Planning the analysis itself. The knowledge area that governs all the others.
overview: Chapter 3 is business analysis about business analysis: how the work will be done, who will be involved, how decisions get made, how information is managed, and how performance is improved. It is deliberately worked late in the twelve weeks, because it is far easier to plan work you now understand.

The first half covers the approach and stakeholder engagement. The distinction to hold is between analysing stakeholders and planning engagement with them: identifying who they are and positioning them by influence and interest is analysis; deciding how often, how formally and by what means you will deal with each is the plan. Producing a map is not having a plan.

tasks.name: Plan Business Analysis Approach
tasks.what: Decide how the analysis will be done: predictive, adaptive or a mix, with the deliverables and formality that follow.
tasks.watch: The approach follows the work. Fixed, externally determined requirements argue for up-front specification whatever the house style.

tasks.name: Plan Stakeholder Engagement
tasks.what: Decide how you will work with each stakeholder, based on who they are and what they need.
tasks.watch: Analysis identifies and positions them; the plan says what you will actually do about each.

concepts.meaning: Two ends of a spectrum, not a binary. Most real work sits somewhere between, and the choice follows the uncertainty in the requirements.
Identifying who is affected and positioning them by influence, interest and attitude.
A characterised user group. Needed when a cohort contains materially different needs that an average would hide.
One way of recording who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed. A device inside the engagement plan, not the plan itself.

traps: Producing a stakeholder map and calling it an engagement plan.
Designing for an average user in a cohort whose groups differ materially.
Choosing the approach by organisational habit rather than by the nature of the work.
Planning engagement when the real problem is that nobody can say where decision rights sit.
prepare: Read 3.1 and 3.2.
Write the approach for a piece of work you are on now, in half a page. Note where you had to guess.
Bring a stakeholder who was missed on a previous engagement, and what it cost.
discuss: Who decides the analysis approach in your organisation — the analyst, or the method?
How do you handle a stakeholder with high influence and no interest?
Where have decision rights moved without anyone recording it?

weeks.title: Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring, part 2
weeks.strap: Governance, information management, and improving the analysis itself.
overview: The second half of chapter 3 covers how decisions about requirements get made and changes controlled, how the analysis information is stored, traced and reused, and how business analysis performance is assessed and improved.

Governance and information management are easily blurred. Governance is about authority: who approves, who is consulted, how change is controlled. Information management is about the artefacts: where they live, how they are traced, how long they are kept and how they get reused. A question about who may approve a change is governance; a question about where the approved version lives is information management.

tasks.name: Plan Business Analysis Governance
tasks.what: Define how decisions are made and how change is controlled.
tasks.watch: Requires knowing where authority actually sits, which is not always what the org chart says.

tasks.name: Plan Business Analysis Information Management
tasks.what: Decide how analysis information is organised, stored, traced, accessed and reused.
tasks.watch: Includes how long things are kept and in what form — the difference between a record and a pile.

tasks.name: Identify Business Analysis Performance Improvements
tasks.what: Assess how the analysis work itself is going and improve it.
tasks.watch: This is about the analysis, not the solution. Requirements churn at three times the norm is a 3.5 finding.

concepts.meaning: Who decides, who is consulted, and how change is controlled.
How the analysis information is organised, traced, retained and reused.
A measure of the analysis work — churn, rework, cycle time, defect origin — not of the solution.
Held while the people who were there still are. Recollection degrades quickly once a team disperses.

traps: Answering a governance question with an information management answer, or the reverse.
Deferring a lessons learned session until benefits data matures, by which time the team has gone.
Measuring the solution when the task asks about the analysis.
Treating a follow-through failure as a facilitation problem.
prepare: Read 3.3 to 3.5.
Find out who is actually authorised to approve a requirement change on your current work. It is often not who you assume.
Bring a lessons learned session that produced nothing, and be ready to say why.
discuss: Where does your analysis information live, and could someone else find it in a year?
How is business analysis performance measured in your organisation, if at all?
What would you change about how change is controlled where you work?

weeks.title: Perspectives
weeks.strap: Five lenses on the same work. Not exclusive, not a house style, and examinable.
overview: The final chapter describes five perspectives on business analysis: agile, business intelligence, information technology, business architecture and business process management. Each shades how the tasks and techniques are applied without replacing them.

Two things carry the exam questions here. First, perspectives are not mutually exclusive — a single change routinely has data, technology, process and capability dimensions at once, and choosing one lens leaves the others unexamined. Second, the approach follows the work rather than the team's habit: legislated rules that are fixed in advance do not want just-in-time elaboration, however the rest of the organisation runs.

tasks.name: Agile
tasks.what: Requirements elaborated just in time, in short cycles, with the analyst helping the team and the product owner understand each other.
tasks.watch: The analyst is not a proxy customer. Deferring detail is not the same as deferring the check that an item can be finished.

tasks.name: Business Intelligence
tasks.what: Specify the decision the information supports, then the data: sources, quality, latency and agreed meaning.
tasks.watch: Two correct figures for the same measure is usually a definition problem, not a data quality defect.

tasks.name: Information Technology
tasks.what: Analysis across the software life cycle, with strong emphasis on quality attributes and the existing landscape.
tasks.watch: Non-functional requirements drive the architecture. Leaving them to the technical team inverts the order.

tasks.name: Business Architecture
tasks.what: The enterprise as the unit of analysis: capabilities, value streams, information and organisation.
tasks.watch: Not solution or technology architecture. A capability view must stand without reference to systems.

tasks.name: Business Process Management
tasks.what: The end-to-end process as the unit of analysis and of ongoing management.
tasks.watch: A process is owned and measured continuously, not improved once by a project that then disbands.

concepts.meaning: Detail added as it is needed. Not licence to skip establishing whether an item is ready to build.
How current the information is. A first-order requirement in business intelligence work, set by the decision it supports.
Investing against what the enterprise must be able to do, rather than against departments or systems.
The whole flow that produces an outcome. Improving a step that is not the constraint moves the queue, not the result.

traps: Choosing a perspective by preference rather than by the work.
Assuming one perspective covers a change that has four dimensions.
Treating a backlog as the record of the current state.
Improving a process fragment and reporting it as an end-to-end gain.
prepare: Read chapter 11.
Take a change you are on and name every perspective that applies. Most have more than one.
Bring an example where the approach was chosen by habit rather than by fit.
discuss: Which perspective does your organisation default to, and what does it miss?
Where have you seen a backlog asked to do the job of a requirements record?
Who owns an end-to-end process in your organisation — genuinely, not nominally?
